text: The tornado outbreak of June 5–6, 2010, impacted the Midwestern United States and parts of the Great Lakes region, beginning on the weekend of June 5 and continuing into the morning of June 6. At least 53 tornadoes were confirmed from Iowa to southern Ontario and Ohio, as well as in northern New England. Seven people were killed in Ohio just outside Toledo in Wood County, and one person died in Dwight, Illinois. Total damage in the United States exceeded $266 million. A low pressure system moved across the central United States on June 5, with a moderate risk for severe thunderstorms issued for areas along Interstate 80 from the Quad Cities to near Cleveland, Ohio, and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Strong storms developed early in the afternoon across the risk area and into central Iowa, with tornadoes reported near Interstate 35 and in parts of central Ohio. Severe weather shifted into Illinois during the early evening as daytime heating and instability peaked, with tornadoes reported in the Peoria area and areas just west of Chicago. Heavy damage occurred in LaSalle County and Livingston County, Illinois, and a tornado emergency was issued in Peoria after multiple sightings. In Streator, an EF2 tornado damaged 180 homes, destroyed 20 homes, and injured 17 people; two additional tornadoes (rated EF0 and EF3) touched down just outside Streator, causing further damage to homes and power lines. In Dwight, a second EF2 tornado struck a mobile home park, destroying 12 homes and rendering several others uninhabitable; other buildings were damaged and several well-built homes lost their roofs. Two EF0 tornadoes also occurred in Dwight, damaging roofs, trees, and derailing a train; six people were injured, one of whom died from injuries by the end of the month. After midnight, storms moved into northern Indiana, northern Ohio, southern Michigan, and southwestern Ontario, with heavy damage reported in Wood County, Ohio, where seven people were killed. In Allen Township, eight homes were destroyed, three received major damage, and 10 received minor damage. Heavy damage was also reported in Leamington, Ontario, where a state of emergency was declared. In Michigan, counties including Calhoun, Kalamazoo, Hillsdale, Jackson, Ingham, Branch, Berrien, Van Buren, Saint Joseph, Washtenaw, Wayne, and Monroe were under simultaneous tornado warnings, including two separate warnings covering all of Calhoun County. Damage in Calhoun County included downed trees and a metal flagpole bent at a right angle in Homer due to extreme winds; tornado sirens were activated in many communities. An EF1 tornado was confirmed just south of Battle Creek, damaging a church roof; an EF2 tornado damaged 311 houses, apartments, and commercial/public buildings in Monroe County. A moderate risk was issued for June 6 along the northeast coast primarily for damaging winds, with tornadoes also a significant threat, but the event mostly resulted in scattered wind damage with no tornadoes. Illinois Governor Pat Quinn declared LaSalle, Livingston, Peoria, and Putnam counties disaster areas. Allegations of racial discrimination arose in mainly African American communities of Pembroke Township and Hopkins Park, as they were not included in the disaster area. Quinn stated that Kankakee County had not requested disaster status for Pembroke. Many residents of Pembroke received no warning before the tornadoes; the community had received a state grant to purchase a tornado siren, but funds were never allocated, leaving the town of 2,784 residents without a warning system. After it was revealed the area had no working siren, state lawmakers Lisa Dugan and Toi Hutchinson pledged to provide weather radios to every home and raise funding for a tornado siren. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) rejected federal disaster aid for victims in Elmwood, Illinois.
